Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Parker-Hannifin Corp" (ticker PH), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",

 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},

                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?

Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?

   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?

   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.

}

result.name: Parker-Hannifin Corporation
result.industry: Motion and control technologies (industrial and aerospace components)
markets: Hydraulics, pneumatics and electromechanical motion control
Fluid connectors: hose, fittings, tubing and couplings
Filtration (industrial, HVAC, life sciences, engine and process)
Engineered materials: seals, gaskets, vibration control and thermal materials
Aerospace systems: flight controls, fuel, hydraulic, engine and braking components

mission.statement: Enabling Engineering Breakthroughs that Lead to a Better Tomorrow
mission.source: Parker company purpose statement (Parker FY25 fact sheet and website)
mission.plain: Parker wants its engineering parts to help customers make breakthroughs that make life better.

about.plain: Parker makes the hidden parts that make machines move and stay under control. These include hoses, pumps, valves, seals, filters and electric motor controls, plus many systems inside airplanes. Factories, farm and construction machines, trucks, planes and labs all use them. Parker is more than 100 years old and sells through thousands of local distributors around the world.
about.customers: Machine and vehicle makers, aircraft makers and airlines, factories and the distributors that serve them buy from Parker.
about.everyday: Parker parts help move the wing flaps and brakes of many passenger jets and the arms of excavators you see on building sites.

money.part: Industrial motion and control parts (Diversified Industrial)
money.plain: hydraulics, hoses and fittings, seals, filters, pneumatics and valves for machines and factories
flight control, fuel, hydraulic and engine parts for planes, plus repairs and spare parts
filters for HVAC, life sciences and factories, mostly replacement filters (about $2B a year of sales)
motor controllers for electric forklifts, carts and work machines

result.summary: Parker has a solid competitive advantage built on a huge range of engineered parts that get designed into customers' machines and aircraft, a global network of about 18,300 distribution outlets, and a strong replacement-parts business. Its Win Strategy operating system has lifted gross margin from 33.1% in FY2021 to 37.7% in FY2026 and adjusted segment margin to 27.3%. Its weaknesses are exposure to industrial cycles and strong rivals such as Bosch Rexroth, Danfoss and Eaton.

pricingPower.evidence: Parker raised margins through a flat-to-down industrial cycle: FY2025 sales slipped 0.4% yet gross margin rose from 35.8% to 36.9%, and FY2026 gross margin reached 37.7% (adjusted segment margin 27.3%, up 120 bps) on 6.6% organic growth, while it offset tariff costs. It does not publish its list-price increases, and much of the margin gain also comes from productivity and portfolio mix.

moats.evidence: Parker is a well-known, trusted name among engineers and distributors, ranked 5th in its industry in Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies, though it is little known by consumers.

Its parts are specified and certified into customers' machines and aircraft platforms for many years, so replacements usually come from Parker; aerospace parts carry FAA certification and aftermarket sales follow for decades, and its aerospace backlog hit a record $8.5B in June 2026.
Its roughly 18,300 distribution outlets gain from the full product range, but users do not make the product more valuable for each other.

With $21.5B of FY2026 sales and 322 plants it is the largest motion-control maker, which spreads purchasing, engineering and distribution costs, though rivals like Bosch Rexroth and Danfoss are also large.
Many of its niches have few qualified suppliers, especially aerospace, but most industrial markets have several capable rivals.
Its business model is the same as its main rivals'.

The Win Strategy operating system (lean, pricing, simplification) helped lift adjusted segment margin to 27.3% in FY2026 and is applied to acquisitions like Meggitt (bought for $7.1B net cash in FY2023), but other industrials run similar systems.
It holds many patents and aircraft certifications, but no exclusive raw material or asset.

customers.evidence: Long relationships through distributors and OEM design-ins keep customers coming back: backlog reached a record $12.8B in June 2026 and Q4 FY2026 orders rose 12% on its new rolling basis; Parker publishes no NPS.

talent.evidence: Parker employs about 58,000 people and is on Fortune's World's Most Admired and America's Most Innovative Companies lists, but it is not a top-tier employer brand for engineers compared with big tech companies.

product.evidence: Parker offers one of the broadest motion and control portfolios in the world (seven technology areas across about 1,000 markets), and its parts fly on most major commercial and military aircraft, though in single product lines such as pneumatics (SMC) or mobile hydraulics (Danfoss, Bosch Rexroth) rivals are equally strong.

threats: A downturn in industrial, construction or farm equipment demand, which makes up most of the Diversified Industrial segment
Integration and debt risk from the $9.25B Filtration Group purchase, funded with $7.75B of term loans in August 2026
A slowdown in commercial aircraft production or airline flying that would hit aerospace original-equipment and aftermarket sales
Electrification of mobile machines and factories replacing hydraulic and pneumatic content with electric drives where rivals such as Bosch Rexroth, Siemens or SMC are strong
Lower-cost Asian competitors in hose, fittings and pneumatics
Tariffs and trade disputes affecting a global supply chain

ceo.name: Jennifer (Jenny) A. Parmentier
ceo.background: Bachelor's in management (Webster University); earlier at Trane/Ingersoll Rand; joined Parker in 2008 and ran the Engineered Materials and Motion Systems groups and served as COO before becoming CEO in January 2023 and chairman in 2024

c1.evidence: Parker leads motion and control, a mature industry growing at low-to-mid single digits (its own FY2031 target is 4%-6% organic growth), not a fast-growing emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Parker for its broad engineered range, design-in support and about 18,300 distribution outlets, and parts certified onto aircraft are hard to displace, but rivals like Bosch Rexroth, Danfoss and SMC offer comparable products.

c3.evidence: Most ordinary people have never heard of Parker; it is well known only among engineers, distributors and investors, though it is a leader in its field.

c4.evidence: Its purpose statement, 'Enabling Engineering Breakthroughs that Lead to a Better Tomorrow', is used across the company, but management communication centers on margins, EPS and cash flow targets.

c6.evidence: “Industrial, reliable, well-run”: among people who know it the impression is positive (a steady, high-quality industrial and dividend payer), but most of the public has no impression at all.

c7.evidence: Its markets are large (aerospace, industrial machinery, filtration) and aerospace and electrification are growing, but most of its addressable market grows with general industrial output rather than a strong secular trend.

c8.evidence: Parker keeps expanding through acquisitions such as Meggitt (aerospace, FY2023), Curtis Instruments (electrification, $1.0B) and Filtration Group ($9.25B, August 2026), but these are adjacent markets rather than big new ones.

m1.evidence: Parmentier has a clear plan, raising the FY2031 adjusted segment margin target to 30% and shifting the portfolio toward aerospace, aftermarket and filtration, but it is an operating vision rather than a transformative picture of the future.

m2.evidence: She is a Parker veteran since 2008 who thinks long term about the portfolio, but she is a hired professional CEO, not a founder.

m4.evidence: Parker stresses safety (FY2026 was its 'safest year ever') and team-based working under the Win Strategy, but there is little public evidence of an unusual servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: The Win Strategy creates a strong, distinctive operating culture focused on safety, productivity and margins, but it is more about execution than inventing new technologies.

m6.evidence: She came up through Parker's operations and product groups (Engineered Materials, Motion Systems), but her degree is in management rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: There is no public sign of misconduct and she is known as a steady leader, but no notable evidence of a mission beyond running the company well.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Parmentier at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university was found.

m8b.evidence: She keeps a low public profile, typical of industrial CEOs, rather than a distinctive, memorable public persona.

m9.evidence: Since she became CEO, diluted EPS rose from $16.04 (FY2023) to $28.48 (FY2026), adjusted segment margin reached 27.3% and Parker has beaten consensus EPS in each of the last six reported quarters.

m10.evidence: The Win Strategy emphasizes lean operations and cost discipline, with SG&A at 16.1% of FY2026 sales, but Parker is not known for frugality in the way Amazon is.

c10.evidence: Its parts quietly help planes fly, food be harvested and factories run around the world, but they are hidden components rather than products that directly change daily life for billions.

p2.evidence: Making certified aerospace and high-pressure motion parts reliably is hard and important, but many industrial products like hoses and fittings can be made by numerous rivals.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew in four of the last five years: $14.35B (FY2021) to $15.86B, $19.07B, $19.93B, $19.85B (-0.4% in FY2025) and $21.50B in FY2026.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 33.1% in FY2021 to 37.7% in FY2026, and gross profit less SG&A rose from 16.4% to 21.6% of sales (with a dip in FY2023 after the Meggitt deal).

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt of $8.5B far exceeded $0.5B of cash but was only about 2 times operating cash flow of $4.36B with $15.4B of equity; the August 2026 term loans of $7.75B have since raised debt sharply.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from $2.58B in FY2021 to $4.36B in FY2026, and segment operating income less corporate costs reached $5.07B in FY2026, up from $4.07B in FY2024.

v1.evidence: Parker is a top supplier with a uniquely broad range, but in no single product line is it clearly the best in a way an ordinary person would understand; rivals such as SMC in pneumatics or Bosch Rexroth in hydraulics are equally strong.

v2.evidence: Parker appears on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies (5th in its industry) and America's Most Innovative Companies lists, but it is not on top 'best places to work' rankings like Glassdoor's top 100.

c5.evidence: If Parker disappeared, aircraft makers and airlines, machine builders and factories would struggle to get critical parts and replacements for years, but end consumers would not notice directly.
